Steadiness
STED-ee-nes
n.
From steady + -ness; steady from Old English stede, “place, position.” Renders the Greek hedraios, “seated, settled, steadfast” (1 Cor 15:58; 7:37; Col 1:23), and ametákinētos, “unmoveable.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Steadiness is the settled, unmoveable, persevering character of the regenerate soul whose foundations have been laid in Christ and whose course through life proceeds without the lurching from emphasis to emphasis, opinion to opinion, fervor to lukewarmness, that marks the unsettled believer. Paul’s great closing line of 1 Corinthians 15 gathers the doctrine: therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Three terms stand together: stedfast (hedraioi, seated, well-anchored), unmoveable (ametákinētoi, not to be shifted), and always abounding—a steadiness that is not stagnation but the abundance-overflow of a fixed and ordered life. Paul commends Timothy similarly: but continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of (2 Tim 3:14)—the steadiness of holding fast what has been received against the constant ecclesial and cultural pressure to drift, novel, or shift. James warns of its opposite: a double minded man is unstable in all his ways. Hebrews names the steadiness of the saint’s anchored hope: which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast (Heb 6:19). The biblical pattern of steadiness has its marks. It is doctrinal: the saint continues in the things he has learned, refuses to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, holds the apostolic deposit faithfully across the years. It is practical: the saint maintains his ordinary disciplines (Word, prayer, gathering, generosity, mortification of sin, exercise of the gifts) across the seasons of life rather than abandoning them at the first cooling. It is emotional: the saint, like the Psalmist, refuses to let his soul be carried up and down by every providential gust, anchored as he is in the unchanging God. And it is moral: the saint walks the same line of integrity at sixty that he walked at thirty, with the inevitable refinement of years adding consistency rather than introducing radical course-changes. Steadiness is therefore not the same as stiffness or rigidity; the steady saint can be supple where Scripture is silent, charitable across secondary differences, growing in grace and knowledge across the years. But on the things Scripture has fixed, the steady saint is unmoveable—and that unmoveableness is the great pastoral and ecclesial gift of the long-faithful Christian to the church and to the watching world.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STEADINESS as the quality of being firm in standing or position; stability; the state of being constant in purpose or pursuit; firmness of mind or purpose; in scripture, the settled, unmoveable, persevering character of the regenerate soul anchored in Christ.

expand to see more

STEADINESS, n. — 1. Firmness of standing or position; a state of being not tottering or easily moved; as the steadiness of a tower. 2. The state of being not subject to change; constancy in purpose or pursuit; perseverance. 3. Firmness of mind or purpose; resolution. 4. Constancy; consistency in moral or religious conduct.

STEADY, a. — Firm in standing or position; fixed; not tottering or shaking; stable. Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord (1 Cor 15:58).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 15:58 — "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

Hebrews 6:19 — "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil."

James 1:6-8 — "But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed... A double minded man is unstable in all his ways."

Colossians 1:23 — "If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Steadiness is corrupted, on one side, by the novelty-chasing register that prizes the new emphasis, the new conference, the new technique, and lurches from focus to focus without settling into the long faithfulness Scripture commends—and on the other by the rigidity-caricature that mistakes mere stiffness for biblical steadiness and refuses growth in grace and knowledge along the way.

expand to see more

The novelty-chasing register is the more visible contemporary corruption. The believer moves from the latest book to the latest podcast to the latest conference to the latest movement, never settling into the patient discipline of holding what has been received and walking the long, ordinary line of faithfulness across the years. Each new emphasis is taken up with enthusiasm, then dropped for the next; the long disciplines (Word, prayer, gathering, generosity) are abandoned when they become routine; the saint reaches sixty with no greater steadiness than he had at thirty, only more bookshelves of dropped enthusiasms. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers the dignity of the long-faithful Christian: continuing in the things which he has learned and has been assured of, anchored in the unchanging gospel, refusing to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, settling into the patient course that abounds across decades.

The opposite corruption is the rigidity-caricature that mistakes mere stiffness for biblical steadiness. The believer refuses to grow in grace and knowledge, refuses to recognize legitimate development of his understanding across the years, refuses to extend charity where Scripture extends it, refuses to soften where Scripture is silent. He calls his rigidity steadiness; Scripture calls it something else. Biblical steadiness is settled on the things Scripture has fixed and supple on the things Scripture has left to liberty; it grows in grace and knowledge across the years; it extends charity across secondary differences; it is the unmoveableness of the well-anchored ship at sea, not the inflexibility of the dead tree on the hill. Recover both ends. Refuse the novelty-chasing that never settles, and refuse the rigidity that mistakes itself for fidelity. The biblical pattern is anchored and growing, settled and supple, faithful across decades and charitable across differences—and the church saturated with such steady saints is the church Scripture commends and the world quietly notices.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hedraios (seated, settled, steadfast—1 Cor 15:58; 7:37; Col 1:23) and ametákinētos (unmoveable); the settled, unmoveable, persevering character of the regenerate soul anchored in Christ across the years.

expand to see more

Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, settled, steadfast (1 Cor 7:37; 15:58; Col 1:23).

Greek ametákinētos (G277) — unmoveable (1 Cor 15:58).

Greek bebaios (G949) — firm, sure, steadfast (Heb 6:19, the anchor sure and stedfast).

Greek aklīnēs (G186) — not inclining, unwavering (Heb 10:23).

Usage

"Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord—the three terms stand together: settled, unmoveable, abundantly fruitful."

"Biblical steadiness is anchored and growing, settled and supple—not the stagnant rigidity that refuses growth in grace and knowledge."

"Novelty-chasing prizes the latest emphasis; rigidity-caricature refuses growth; biblical steadiness is long faithfulness anchored in the gospel and supple where Scripture is silent."
